'''''Allocasuarina verticillata''''', commonly known as '''drooping sheoak''',<ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Allocasuarina verticillata'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Allocasuarina%20verticillata |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Casuarinaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to south-eastern Australia. It is a small [[Dioecy|dioecious]] tree that has drooping branchlets up to {{cvt|400|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to scales in whorls of nine to thirteen, the mature fruiting cones {{cvt|20–50|mm|sigfig=1}} long containing winged seeds ([[Samara (fruit)|samaras]]) {{cvt|7–12|mm|sigfig=1}} long.

==Description==
''Allocasuarina verticillata'' is a small dioecious tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|4–10|m}}, has fissured bark, and the penultimate branchlets are woody. The branchlets are up to {{cvt|400|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to spreading teeth {{cvt|0.7–1.2|mm|sigfig=1}} long, usually arranged in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of nine to thirteen around the branchlets. The sections of branchlet between the leaf whorls are {{cvt|15–40|mm|sigfig=1}} long, {{cvt|0.7–1.5|mm|sigfig=1}} in diameter but broader at the end near the teeth. Male flowers are arranged in spikes {{cvt|30–120|mm|sigfig=1}} long, with about 2.5 to 4 whorls per cm (per 0.4 in), the [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] {{cvt|1.2–2.5|mm|sigfig=1}} long. Female cones are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] up to {{cvt|10|mm|sigfig=1}} long, and the mature cones are cylindrical to barrel-shaped, {{cvt|25–50|mm|sigfig=1}} long and {{cvt|17–30|mm|sigfig=1}} in diameter, containing dark brown, winged seeds (samaras) {{cvt|7–12|mm|sigfig=1}} long. Flowering occurs in all months.<ref name="foa" /><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Entwisle |first1=Timothy J. |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |title=''Allocasuarina verticillata'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/08e8dacc-5804-4ce7-9dec-f3e34960d801 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Allocasuarina verticillata'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Allocasuarina~verticillata |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="SA">{{cite web |title=''Allocasuarina verticillata'' |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Allocasuarina_verticillata |publisher=State Herbarium of South Australia |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
Drooping sheoak was first formally described in 1788 by French naturalist [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]], who gave it the name ''Casuarina verticillata'' in ''[[Encyclopédie Méthodique|Encyclopédie Méthodique, Botanique]]'' from a tree grown in the [[Jardin du Roi]].<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Casuarina verticillata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/459430 |publisher=APNI|access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="Lam.">{{cite book |last1=Lamarck |first1=Jean-Baptiste |editor-last1=Poiret |editor-first1=Jean L.M. |title=Encyclopédie Méthodique, Botanique |date=1788 |publisher=Panckoucke |location=Paris, Liège |page=501 |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/9708/?offset=#page=505&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q= |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref> In 1982, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] transferred the species to ''Allocasuarina'' as ''A. verticillata'' in the ''[[Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Allocasuarina verticillata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/499455|publisher=APNI|access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="JABG">{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Lawrence A.S. |title=Notes on Casuarinaceae II. |journal=Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens |date=1982 |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=79 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/61978679#page/91/mode/1up |access-date=24 August 2023}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''verticillata'' means 'having whorls'.<ref name="Sharr">{{cite book |last1=Sharr |first1=Francis Aubi |last2=George |first2=Alex |title=Western Australian Plant Names and Their Meanings |date=2019 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, WA |isbn=978-0-9580341-8-0 |page=335 |edition=3rd}}</ref>

The 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'' records common names of the plant, including shingle oak, coast she-oak, river oak, salt-water swamp oak, and that it was called ''worgnal'' by the indigenous people of the [[Richmond River|Richmond]] and [[Clarence River (New South Wales)|Clarence River]] areas of New South Wales. It also records that "In cases of severe thirst, great relief may be obtained from chewing the foliage of this and other species, which, being of an acid nature, produces a flow of saliva — a fact well-known to bushmen who have traversed waterless portions of the country. This acid is closely allied to citric acid, and may prove identical with it. Children chew the young cones, which they call 'oak apples'."<ref>{{cite book | author=J. H. Maiden | year=1889 | title=The useful native plants of Australia: Including Tasmania | publisher= Turner and Henderson, Sydney | url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Allocasuarina verticillata'' usually grows in grassy woodland, sometimes forming pure stands and sometimes with eucalypts. It is also found on rocky sea coasts and on dry ridges inland. In New South Wales it occurs on rocky hills south from [[Cobar]] and on coastal shale south from [[Sydney]]. It is widespread in Victoria, extending westwards to the [[Flinders Ranges]], [[Gawler Ranges]], western [[Eyre Peninsula]] and [[Kangaroo Island]] in South Australia. In Tasmania, the species is found near [[Launceston, Tasmania|Launceston]] and on the east coast as far south as [[Hobart]] and the [[Tasman Peninsula]].<ref name="foa" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="SA" /><ref name="utas">{{cite web |last1=Jordan |first1=Greg |title=''Allocasuarina verticillata'' |url=https://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/Fagales/sAllocasuarina_verticillata.htm |publisher=University of Tasmania |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[Aboriginal Australians]] make use of the tree for a range of tasks.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ngunnawal Elders |title=Ngunnawal Plant Use |publisher=ACT Government |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-921117-15-2 |edition=2nd |location=Canberra |page=14 |language=EN}}</ref>  The [[Ngunnawal]] people make tools including [[boomerang]]s from the tree's timber.<ref name=":0" />  Mature [[Infructescence|cones]] are used as [[Toy|children's toys]].<ref name=":0" />  

== Ecology ==
On Kangaroo Island, ''A. verticillata'' is the preferred food of the [[glossy black cockatoo]], which holds the cones in its foot and shreds them with its powerful bill before removing the seeds with its tongue.<ref name="Austral">{{cite journal |last1=Crowley |first1=Gabriel M. |last2=Garnett |first2=Stephen T. |title=Food value and tree selection by Glossy Black-Cockatoos ''Calyptorhynchus lathami'' |journal=Austral Ecology |date=2001 |volume=26 |issue=1 |page=116–126 |doi=10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01093.pp.x |url=https://researchers.cdu.edu.au/en/publications/food-value-and-tree-selection-by-glossy-black-cockatoos-calyptorh/ |access-date=7 December 2025}}</ref>

==Biochemistry==
[[Pedunculagin]], [[casuarictin]], [[strictinin]], [[casuarinin]] and [[casuariin]] are [[ellagitannins]], which have been found in this species.<ref name="J.Chem.Soc.">{{cite journal |last1=Okuda |first1=Takuo |last2=Yoshida |first2=Takashi |last3=Ashida |first3=Mariko |last4=Yazaki |first4=Kazufumi |title=Tannins of ''Casuarina'' and ''Stachyurus'' species. I: Structures of pendunculagin, casuarictin, strictinin, casuarinin, casuariin, and stachyurin |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 1 |date=1983 |volume=1 |pages=1765–1772 |doi=10.1039/P19830001765 |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1983/p1/p19830001765 |access-date=7 December 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
